entries.meaning: Even so my teacher told it repeatedly; I understood only as much as my understanding allowed. I shall bind that same story in the people’s language so that my own mind may awaken. With whatever intellect, discernment and strength I possess, I will tell it in my heart under Hari’s prompting. I compose the story that removes my doubts, delusion and error and serves as a boat across the river of becoming. Rāma’s story is repose for the wise, delight for everyone and destroyer of Kali’s stain. It is a peahen that overcomes the serpent of Kali, and the fire-drill for kindling discernment’s flame; the wish-granting cow in Kali and a beautiful life-restoring herb for the virtuous. On earth it is a river of nectar, remover of fear and a serpentess that swallows the frog of delusion. It destroys hell like an army crushing demons and benefits the family of saints and gods like the Mountain’s daughter. For the ocean-like community of saints it is Lakṣmī; like the steadfast, forgiving Earth it bears the world’s burden. It is Yamunā to blacken Yama’s attendants’ faces, and like Kāśī it is a means to life and liberation. It is dear to Rāma and purifying like tulasī, and for Tulsīdāsa it blossoms joyfully within the heart. It is dear to Śiva like Narmadā, daughter of Mount Mekala, and a treasury of all accomplishment, happiness and wealth. It is Aditi, mother of the gods who are good qualities, and the very summit of love for Raghubara’s devotion. Rāma’s story is Mandākinī, the beautiful mind is Citrakūṭa, and Tulsī’s lovely affection is the forest where Sītā and Raghubīra roam.

Rāma’s deeds are a lovely wish-fulfilling jewel and the beautiful adornment of the bride who is saintly understanding. The clusters of Rāma’s virtues bring auspiciousness to the world and bestow liberation, wealth, dharma and its abiding place. They are true teachers of knowledge, detachment and yoga, and divine physicians for the terrible disease of worldly existence. They are mother and father of love for Sītā and Rāma, and seeds of every vow, dharma and discipline. They calm sin, torment and grief, and lovingly sustain this world and the next. They are ministers, warriors and king of right reflection, and Agastya to the boundless ocean of greed. They are lion cubs against the elephant-herds of desire, anger and Kali’s stain, dwelling in the forest of devotees’ minds. They are honoured guests, supremely dear to Śiva, and wish-granting clouds that drive poverty from the door. They are mantra and great jewel against serpents of sense-objects, erasing hard, inauspicious marks written on the forehead. They are rays of the sun that remove delusion’s darkness and rain-clouds that nurture servants as rice plants. They grant cherished wishes like the finest celestial tree, and are as accessible and joy-giving in service as Hari and Hara. To fine poets they are stars in the autumn sky of the mind, and to Rāma’s devotees their very wealth of life. They are the fruit of every meritorious act, abundant enjoyments, and saints who selflessly benefit the world. They are swans in the Mānas lake of servants’ minds, purifying like fire and a garland of Gaṅgā’s waves. Rāma’s clusters of virtues burn wrong paths, false reasoning, misconduct, Kali’s deceit, pride and hypocrisy as a fierce fire consumes fuel. Rāma’s deeds are soothing like full-moon rays to everyone, bringing special welfare and great gain to saintly hearts, lotus-like and cātaka-like.

I shall sing and explain the whole occasion: how Bhavānī asked her question and how Śaṅkara answered it, shaping the narrative in a wondrous way. Anyone who has not heard this story should not be astonished on hearing it. The wise who hear a supernatural tale do not marvel, knowing that Rāma’s story has no measure in the world. Many are Rāma’s descents, and the Rāmāyaṇas are boundless—numbered in hundreds of crores. In different cosmic cycles, sages have sung Hari’s beautiful deeds in many ways. Therefore bring no doubt into the heart; listen to the story with love for Sarasvatī. Rāma is infinite, his virtues infinite, and the story immeasurably extensive; those whose reflection is pure will not be astonished on hearing it.

Having removed every doubt in this way and placed the dust of the teacher’s lotus feet upon my head, I again petition everyone with joined hands, so that no fault may attach to my telling. Reverently bowing my head to Śiva, I now describe the stainless account of Rāma’s virtues. In Vikrama year sixteen hundred and thirty-one I begin the story, placing my head at Hari’s feet. On the ninth lunar day, a Tuesday in the month of Madhu, this narrative became manifest in Ayodhyā. On that day, which the Veda celebrates as Rāma’s birth, all sacred places come there. Asuras, nāgas, birds, humans, sages and gods arrive to serve Raghunāyaka. The wise arrange the birth festival and sing Rāma’s beautiful fame. Crowds of good people bathe in the deeply purifying water of Sarayū and repeat Rāma’s name, holding in the heart through meditation his beautiful dark-hued form.

Seeing, touching, bathing in and drinking Sarayū’s water removes sin, say the Vedas and Purāṇas. The river is holy, immeasurable in greatness; even pure-minded Sarasvatī cannot describe it. The lovely city grants Rāma’s abode and is known throughout all worlds as supremely holy. Countless creatures of the four modes of birth who leave their bodies in Ayodhyā do not return to worldly existence. Knowing the city to be enchanting in every way, grantor of all accomplishments and mine of auspiciousness, I begin the stainless story, whose hearing destroys desire, pride and hypocrisy. Its name is Rāmacaritamānasa; hearing it with the ears brings repose. The mind, burning like a forest in the fire of sense-objects, becomes happy if it falls into this lake. Śiva fashioned within his mind the lovely, purifying Rāmacaritamānasa that delights sages. It drives away threefold fault, suffering and poverty and destroys Kali’s misconduct and deep impurity. Having composed it, Maheśa kept it in his own mind and, finding a good occasion, told it in speech to Śivā. Therefore, joyfully beholding it in his heart, Hara gave it the excellent name Rāmacaritamānasa. I tell that same pleasing and beautiful story; good people, listen reverently with attentive minds. Now, remembering Umā and bull-bannered Śiva, I tell the whole occasion—how this Mānasa came to be and why it spread in the world.
